headline: Amazon Wants to Track Every Product Sold Online — Even Ones It Doesn't Sell

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Amazon is a huge online store. Now it wants to build a giant list of every product sold anywhere on the internet, not just things Amazon sells. This plan is called the 'World Product Graph.' Why would Amazon do this? Right now, if you want to find a product, you might search on Google or ask questions on Reddit. Amazon wants you to stay on its own website instead. It also wants its shopping helper robot, called Alexa for Shopping, to give better answers. Right now, this robot sometimes gets facts wrong. Having more information could help it answer questions correctly. This plan could also help when people use AI helpers to shop for them. If Amazon has the biggest list of products, those AI helpers might send shoppers to Amazon more often. Amazon says this idea is still just a draft, and it might not happen. A document about it mentioned a date in 2027, but nothing is certain yet.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Amazon is working on a big project called the 'World Product Graph.' The idea is to collect information about every product sold online, even items that other stores sell instead of Amazon. According to a news report from Reuters, Amazon wants to use this giant collection of data to keep shoppers on its own website instead of letting them search elsewhere, like on Google or Reddit, to compare products. Amazon already lets some outside store links show up on its site through a feature called 'shop direct.' The company also uses an AI assistant called Alexa for Shopping, which used to be called Rufus, to help customers shop. However, an internal company document reportedly said this AI often gives wrong or incomplete answers, and running it is costly. Amazon hopes that adding tons of extra product data will make the AI smarter, cheaper to run, and more accurate. This project could also affect how other AI shopping assistants work. If Amazon ends up having the largest and most complete database of products anywhere, those other AI tools might rely on Amazon's information too, sending even more shoppers to Amazon's site. To build this database, Amazon might need to scan other companies' websites to figure out how they list their products. It is still unclear if this plan will actually happen. Amazon said the leaked document was just an early brainstorm, not a confirmed plan, even though it mentioned a possible 2027 launch date.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: A new report from Reuters reveals that Amazon is developing a project called the 'World Product Graph,' designed to create a massive database containing information about nearly every product sold online, including items sold by competitors rather than Amazon itself. The goal is to make Amazon the go-to place for shopping research, reducing the need for customers to search elsewhere, such as on Google or Reddit, when they want to compare products or read reviews before buying something. This strategy builds on features Amazon has already introduced, like 'shop direct,' which links to outside retailers directly from Amazon's site, and its AI shopping assistant, currently called Alexa for Shopping (previously named Rufus). According to the leaked internal document, this AI assistant has a real weakness: it frequently produces answers that are wrong or incomplete, and running its searches is expensive for Amazon. By feeding the AI a much larger and more complete pool of shopping data, Amazon hopes to make its answers more reliable while also using less costly technology to generate them. There's a bigger strategic reason behind this plan, too. As more people start using AI agents, computer programs that can browse the internet and make purchases on their behalf, these tools need reliable data sources to find and compare products. If Amazon builds the largest and most trusted product database in the world, AI shopping agents from any company might end up relying on Amazon's information by default. That would mean even shoppers who never intended to use Amazon could still be guided toward its listings. However, actually building this database presents challenges. The internal document notes that the project depends on figuring out how different brands organize and categorize their products on their own websites, which could require Amazon to systematically scan, or 'crawl,' other companies' websites to gather that data. It remains uncertain whether this project will actually launch, despite a mentioned target date of October 2027. Amazon responded to the report by stating that draft documents like this one represent early brainstorming rather than confirmed plans, and don't necessarily reflect what the company will actually do going forward.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: According to a Reuters report, Amazon is developing an ambitious project internally called the 'World Product Graph,' which aims to compile a comprehensive database of product information from across the entire internet, not just items Amazon sells. The strategic purpose is clear: keep shoppers within Amazon's ecosystem rather than letting them wander off to research products on platforms like Google or Reddit, and ensure that even searches for products sold exclusively by other retailers still funnel customers back toward Amazon's own pages. This expands on existing features, including 'shop direct,' which already links to external retailers' products from within Amazon's site, and the company's AI shopping assistant, now called Alexa for Shopping and formerly known as Rufus. The internal document reportedly acknowledges a significant problem: the AI assistant often generates answers that are factually incorrect or incomplete, and processing the searches needed to answer customer questions is costly to run at scale. Amazon believes that dramatically increasing the volume and breadth of product data available to the system could solve both problems simultaneously, improving accuracy while also allowing the company to rely on less expensive computing models to generate responses. There's also a longer-term competitive angle driving this effort. As artificial intelligence agents, automated programs capable of browsing the web and completing purchases on a person's behalf, become more common, they will need trustworthy sources of product data to do their jobs effectively. If Amazon manages to build the largest, most authoritative index of products anywhere online, these AI agents, regardless of which company creates them, might default to relying on Amazon's data when making recommendations or completing transactions. That outcome would extend Amazon's influence over online shopping even among people who never intentionally choose to shop through Amazon's platform directly. Still, significant obstacles stand between this idea and actual implementation. The internal document specifies that the project's success hinges on Amazon figuring out how various brands structure and categorize their products on their own independent websites, a task that could require Amazon to systematically crawl, or automatically scan, competitors' sites to extract that information, raising questions about fairness and data use. Reuters notes that it remains genuinely unclear whether or when this plan might move forward, even though the leaked document reportedly listed a target release date of October 1st, 2027. In response to the report, Amazon downplayed its significance, stating that draft and outdated internal documents often present an incomplete picture and that having a brainstorming document doesn't necessarily reflect the company's actual current plans or intentions.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: A Reuters report sheds light on an ambitious internal Amazon initiative known as the 'World Product Graph,' a project aimed at constructing a sweeping database cataloging virtually every product sold anywhere online, regardless of whether Amazon itself sells that item. The underlying strategy is to consolidate Amazon's position as the default destination for product research, discouraging consumers from turning to alternative resources like Google searches or Reddit discussion threads, while simultaneously ensuring that searches for products exclusive to competing retailers still redirect traffic toward Amazon's own platform. This initiative extends existing efforts, such as the 'shop direct' feature introduced last year, which already embeds links to external retailers within Amazon's interface, and the company's evolving AI shopping assistant, currently branded Alexa for Shopping after previously being known as Rufus. Notably, the internal planning document reportedly admits a substantial flaw in the current system: many of the AI assistant's responses are factually inaccurate or incomplete, and the computational cost of processing customer search queries through the AI is considerable. Amazon's proposed solution is to dramatically broaden the scope of product data feeding the system, theoretically improving both the reliability of its answers and the efficiency of the underlying technology, potentially allowing cheaper computing models to produce equally or more accurate results. Beyond fixing an immediate technical shortcoming, this project reflects a broader competitive calculation about the future of commerce. As autonomous AI agents, software capable of independently researching and purchasing products on behalf of human users, become increasingly prevalent, these systems will require dependable, comprehensive data sources to function effectively. Should Amazon succeed in assembling the most extensive and authoritative product index available anywhere, AI agents developed by any company might gravitate toward relying on Amazon's data by default, subtly cementing Amazon's centrality within online retail even for transactions that bypass its platform entirely. This represents a strategic bid to maintain relevance and influence as shopping behavior shifts away from direct browser searches and toward automated, AI-mediated transactions. Nevertheless, considerable uncertainty surrounds whether this vision will materialize. The internal document reportedly states that the project's feasibility depends on Amazon successfully reverse-engineering how various brands structure and categorize products across their own independent websites, a process that would likely necessitate systematically crawling, or automatically scanning, competitors' sites to extract usable data. This raises potential questions about competitive fairness and the appropriate boundaries of data collection practices among rival businesses. Reuters emphasizes that it remains unclear if or when this ambitious plan might actually be implemented, despite the leaked document reportedly specifying a target release date of October 1st, 2027. In its official response, Amazon sought to minimize the report's significance, characterizing the document as an outdated draft and asserting that the mere existence of a brainstorming document doesn't necessarily indicate the company's current strategic direction or confirmed future plans.

questions: If Amazon collects information about every product sold online, how might that change the way you or your family search for things to buy?
Do you think it's fair for one company to gather data from other companies' websites to build something like this? Why or why not?
As AI tools become more common for shopping, how might that change the kinds of skills or knowledge people need to be smart consumers?
